subject.name: Prompted
subject.description: A multiplayer music game in which a Judge sets a prompt, other players answer it with one YouTube video each, everyone votes, and a winner is scored. This model records what the project's own documents claim, reconciled against what the code actually does.

excluded: web-app/test-results/ and web-app/playwright-report/ - 1,661 generated Playwright trace artifacts
server/.env and web-app/.env - confirmed present, deliberately never opened, no value read or quoted
server/prompted.db and its WAL files - live data, not source

actors.name: Player
actors.description: A signed-in person who joins groups, answers prompts and votes.

actors.name: Host
actors.description: The group's creator. Starts rounds and edits rules. Documented and implemented, but the documents do not mention that the role can never be transferred.

actors.name: Judge
actors.description: One player per round who sets the prompt and may name a winner outright. The documents call this the Card Czar. The code calls it czar internally, Judge in player-facing text, and Round Leader in comments.

actors.name: Jury
actors.description: The documents' name for every non-Judge player. The code has no such concept as a distinct role; it simply excludes the Judge from submitting.

workflows.name: Documented game flow
steps: Topic selection by the Card Czar
Voting by all players including the Czar

source.note: Matches the implemented phase order. The music source and the entity names do not match.

workflows.name: Implemented round flow
steps: Host starts and the Judge is chosen

businessRules.rule: A round needs at least two group members, counted by membership and never by who is currently connected.
The Judge may not submit a video.

source.note: Consistent with the documents, which say only the jury submits.

businessRules.rule: The Judge may vote, alongside naming a winner outright.

source.note: Handler comment states this is deliberate. Both documents agree that all players including the Czar vote.

businessRules.rule: Nobody may vote for their own submission, enforced on the server rather than only in the interface.

source.note: Proven by a hand-crafted socket payload in the test suite.

businessRules.rule: A winner is resolved by public override first, then the Judge's selection, then the highest tally.

source.note: The documents describe override and Czar selection but not the precedence between them.

businessRules.rule: A public topic is visible only to people you share a group with, never app-wide.

source.note: The documents describe public topics as available to all games, which is the opposite.

operatingContext.item: The server refuses to boot if AUTH_TEST_MODE is set while NODE_ENV is production.
Outside production the server boots in a degraded mode with loud warnings when credentials are missing, so the suite and a fresh clone both work before any secret exists.
A YouTube search costs 100 of 10,000 daily quota units, which is why results are cached and the test suite runs on fixtures.

product.documentedAs: Game, with a separate join code and a lobby browser

product.definition: One prompt, its submissions, its votes and its result. Called currentTheme in the code.
A prompt, owned by the player who wrote it.
The player who sets the prompt and may pick the winner.
product.state: renamed, but inconsistently in the code itself

system.state: current, but nearly every event name differs

design.definition: The Judge's identity is withheld from the payload, not merely hidden in the interface.
The only implemented topic-selection mode. Three others are commented out with their design intent preserved.

evidence.note: A complete integration with quota handling.

decisions.note: Settled in the code. No document records the change or the reason.

decisions.decision: Persist to SQLite rather than PostgreSQL.
decisions.note: The documents' goal of durable state was met; the named mechanism was not.

decisions.decision: Only Judge Selects ships as a topic-selection mode.

evidence.note: The three alternatives are commented out with the mechanics each would need.

decisions.note: The clearest recorded decision in the codebase. It states what is deferred and why, rather than deleting the idea.

decisions.decision: Gate a round on membership rather than on who is connected, and enforce the submission deadline on interaction rather than by a timer.

evidence.note: Membership gate and its recorded reasoning.
advanceIfExpired: the interaction-driven deadline seam that resolves the prior stall.
The design record choosing the no-scheduler seam and rejecting the timer alternative.

decisions.note: The membership gate is deliberate and documented in a comment. It no longer creates a permanent stall: advanceIfExpired re-arms or advances the round when the deadline passes at an interaction moment.

decisions.decision: Scope a public topic to groupmates rather than the whole app.
decisions.note: Directly contradicts the documents, and is the better privacy model.

decisions.decision: Ship a React Native mobile application.

evidence.note: Described with a concrete file layout and install steps.

decisions.note: Cannot tell from the sources whether this was abandoned or never started.
A setting for it is still collected by the wizard, which suggests a placeholder rather than a removal.

claims.claim: The backend keeps game state in memory and there are no persistent user accounts.
A React Native and Expo application exists under src/.
All players including the Card Czar vote on submissions.

evidence.note: cast_vote has no Judge exclusion and its comment says so deliberately.

claims.claim: The Card Czar's identity is hidden until the round ends.

evidence.note: Enforced by withholding the id from the payload.

claims.claim: Scoring defaults are five points for the Czar's pick and up to three for a jury vote, with a downvote costing one.
A seventy percent public vote can override the Czar's choice.

evidence.note: The threshold is also validated to 51-100, which the documents do not mention.

claims.claim: Public topics are available to all games.

evidence.note: Deliberately scoped to shared groups instead.

claims.claim: Players can skip being Card Czar.
The environment examples describe the operative configuration.

conflicts.description: Both narrative documents describe a different music source, a different database, a different identity provider, a different entity vocabulary and an application that does not exist. The environment examples, by contrast, are accurate.
conflicts.significance: Anyone onboarding from README.md or GAME_DESIGN.md would build the wrong thing. Because the env examples are correct, the problem is specific to the two hand-written documents rather than to the project's documentation as a whole.

conflicts.description: README.md contradicts itself about Spotify, describing it as the current submission mechanism and, in two other sections, as an unbuilt future enhancement.
conflicts.significance: The document was already internally inconsistent before the implementation diverged from it, so its present tense cannot be trusted anywhere.

conflicts.description: One role carries three names. Player-facing text says Judge, internal identifiers say czar, comments say Round Leader, and both documents say Card Czar.
conflicts.significance: This is not simply stale documentation: the implementation has not settled either. Every conversation and every code search about the role is ambiguous.

conflicts.description: The documents describe public topics as available across all games; the implementation deliberately restricts them to groups you share.
conflicts.significance: The implementation is the better privacy model and is pinned by tests, so the document is what should change. Worth recording because it is a design improvement, not a drift.

conflicts.description: The Create Group wizard collects 21 settings. The server reads nine. Nine more change nothing anywhere, and one is enforced only in the client.
conflicts.significance: A host can set a player cap, a round count, a voting time limit, chat, song previews, skip-Judge, custom topics and voter identity, and none take effect. Nothing in the interface distinguishes these from the settings that work.

conflicts.description: Leave Group and Delete Group confirm with the user and then only navigate away.
conflicts.significance: The interface promises an irreversible action and delivers nothing. Neither a client event nor a server handler exists for either.

evidence.note: 15 events, none for leave or delete.

conflicts.description: The submission deadline is now enforced, but only when someone interacts with the group, and there is no deadline on the voting phase.
conflicts.significance: advanceIfExpired evaluates the deadline at natural moments (join, group read, submit, start, and a client countdown nudge). A quiet group whose deadline passes simply does not advance until someone pings it, and a round can still hang in voting because votingTime is never read and close_submissions only works during submission.

evidence.note: The only exit from the submission phase.

gaps: No document explains why Spotify became YouTube, or PostgreSQL became SQLite. Both are settled in code and unrecorded in prose.
No document describes the phase model, the information-hiding rules, or the authorization model, which are the most carefully built parts of the system.
Nothing states whether a group is meant to end after totalRounds or run indefinitely as a standing league.
Nothing records whether the nine inert settings are unfinished work or leftovers.
Repository history is too shallow to date most decisions; where a decision is not captured in a code comment, it usually cannot be recovered.
unresolvedQuestions: Should the Judge both vote and hold an outright winner pick? The code and the documents agree that they may, but nothing records whether the combination was weighed.
Is a downvote meant to cost the voter points as well as dock the target submission? Both happen today.
Was the skip-Judge rotation dropped deliberately, or never built? Its setting is still collected.
What should the role finally be called?
Does the documented React Native application exist anywhere outside this repository?
